# Verified — design tokens as the handoff format

**Date:** 2026-08-01
**Source:** the Design Tokens Format Module, read off the rendered spec (84,421 characters).

`DIRECTION.md` is prose. Spec v2 added `tokens.json` as its machine-readable sibling so the
build step does not have to OCR a design image or parse English. This is what that file must
conform to.

---

## Status — get the name right

It is a **Community Group Draft**, dated **30 July 2026**. It is *not* a W3C Recommendation
and not a W3C standard. Calling it "the W3C design token standard" in the plugin would be
wrong in the same checkable way as the 44pt claim.

Correct phrasing: *the Design Tokens Community Group (DTCG) format*.

Being a live draft two days old is an argument for pinning: state which draft the plugin
targets, because the value shapes below have already changed between drafts.

## The structure rules

Three properties carry everything: `$value`, `$type`, `$description`. `$extensions` holds
tool-specific data.

The one hard structural constraint:

> If an object contains both `$value` and child tokens/groups, this creates an invalid
> structure where the object cannot be both a token and a group.

So `color.brand` cannot be both a color *and* a namespace holding `color.brand.hover`. That
forces a naming decision at design time — either `color.brand.base` / `color.brand.hover`, or
a flat leaf. Worth stating, because the intuitive nesting is illegal.

`$type` is inherited from the nearest ancestor group that declares it, which is why grouping
by type rather than by component is the cheaper structure.

## The type list — verified, exhaustive

`border` · `cubicBezier` · `dimension` · `duration` · `fontFamily` · `fontWeight` ·
`gradient` · `number` · `shadow` · `strokeStyle` · `transition` · `typography`

(Plus `color`, whose section uses different phrasing than the "MUST be set to the string X"
construction the others share — its exact value shape was not confirmed in this pass and needs
one more look before we write a color token by hand.)

## The two value shapes that break naive token files

**`dimension` is an object, not a string.**

> The value MUST be an object containing a numeric value (integer or floating-point) and unit
> of measurement (**"px" or "rem"**).

So `"16px"` is invalid. It must be `{ "value": 16, "unit": "px" }`. And the unit set is closed
— **px and rem only**. No `pt`, no `dp`, no `em`, no `%`.

**This collides directly with our platform research.** Apple specifies in `pt`, Material in
`dp` and `sp`. Neither is expressible in a DTCG `dimension`. So `tokens.json` is a **web
artifact**, and native surfaces need their numbers carried in `DIRECTION.md` prose or in a
`$extensions` block. That is a real limit of the handoff format and the plugin should say so
rather than pretending one file serves all four surfaces.

**`duration` is likewise an object**, numeric value plus `"ms"` or `"s"`.

## Composite types are the useful part

`typography`, `shadow`, `border`, `transition`, `gradient`, and `strokeStyle` are composite —
one token carrying several sub-values. That maps well onto what Gate B actually produces: a
motion spec is a set of `transition` tokens (duration + `cubicBezier` + delay), not a
paragraph.

Aliasing supports **pointer syntax into a composite** — "references to specific properties
within composite tokens, not just entire token values" — so a design system can reuse one
easing curve across every transition without duplicating it.

## What this settles for the plugin

1. **`tokens.json` targets a pinned DTCG draft**, named by date, and is described as a
   Community Group format rather than a standard.
2. **It is web-scoped.** Native `pt`/`dp`/`sp` values live in `DIRECTION.md` and optionally
   `$extensions`. Say the limit out loud.
3. **Group by type, not by component**, so `$type` inherits and the file stays short.
4. **Paired color tokens** — the `minimalist-ui` steal where a swatch ships with its
   foreground — need modelling as a group of two color tokens with a `$description` binding
   them, since DTCG has no native "pair" type. Contrast stays structural, but the pairing is a
   convention we impose, not one the format enforces.
5. **The motion spec becomes `transition` tokens**, which is the first time in this family a
   motion spec has been machine-readable instead of prose that gets rebuilt three times.

## Still open

The `color` value shape (colorSpace, hex vs components), and whether any real tooling consumes
this draft's object-form `dimension` yet — a format nothing reads is a format that will drift.

1	# Verified — native mobile design law
2	
3	**Date:** 2026-08-01
4	**Method:** rendered DOM read off the live primary sources with a headless browser.
5	
6	---
7	
8	## First: a third fabrication, and what it means for the cached claims
9	
10	The dead mobile research run extracted a claim attributing this to Apple's Materials page:
11	
12	> "When placing elements on top of Liquid Glass, avoid applying the material to both layers.
13	> Instead, use fills, transparency, and vibrancy for the top elements to make them feel like a
14	> thin overlay that is part of the material."
15	
16	and defined Liquid Glass as *"a translucent surface that reflects and refracts light."*
17	
18	Checked against the live page (17,870 characters of rendered text):
19	
20	| Phrase | Occurrences |
21	|---|---|
22	| "both layers" | **0** |
23	| "on top of Liquid Glass" | **0** |
24	| "thin overlay" | **0** |
25	| "reflects and refracts" | **0** |
26	| "vibrancy" | 24 |
27	
28	The page genuinely discusses vibrancy, so the claim is *plausible* and may paraphrase real
29	guidance elsewhere in Apple's docs. But **the quoted wording does not exist on the page it was
30	attributed to.** That is the third instance of this failure — the completed WCAG run caught two
31	others and warned that "every quotation in the final deliverable must be re-derived from raw
32	W3C HTML."
33	
34	**Standing rule for this project:** no quotation ships in the plugin unless it was read off the
35	rendered primary source. The 353 claims in `_mobile-raw-claims.md` and `_weba11y-raw-claims.md`
36	are leads, not evidence.
37	
38	---
39	
40	## Liquid Glass — verified
41	
42	Apple platforms have **two** material types: Liquid Glass, and standard materials.
43	
44	> Liquid Glass forms a distinct functional layer for controls and navigation — like tab bars and
45	> sidebars — that floats above the content layer, establishing a clear visual hierarchy between
46	> functional elements and content.
47	
48	### The hard rules, in Apple's words
49	
50	> **Don't use Liquid Glass in the content layer.** Liquid Glass works best when it provides a
51	> clear distinction between the functional layer and the content layer.
52	
53	> **Use Liquid Glass effects sparingly.** Standard components… pick up the appearance and
54	> behavior of this material automatically. If you apply Liquid Glass effects to a custom
55	> control, do so sparingly. Liquid Glass seeks to bring attention to the underlying content, and
56	> overusing this material can distract from important functional elements.
57	
58	So it is a **navigation-and-controls material only**, applied automatically by standard
59	components, and deliberately used sparingly on custom ones. A design that renders content cards
60	in Liquid Glass is violating the primary rule of the material.
61	
62	### Two variants, and the choice between them is a decision procedure
63	
64	| Variant | What it does | When |
65	|---|---|---|
66	| **Regular** | "blurs and adjusts the luminosity of background content to maintain legibility of text and other foreground elements" | when background content **might create legibility issues**, or when components carry significant text — *alerts, sidebars, popovers* |
67	| **Clear** | lets rich content through for immersion | **only** for components over **visually rich backgrounds** — photos, video |
68	
69	> **Only use clear Liquid Glass for components that appear over visually rich backgrounds.**
70	
71	And clear carries a follow-on decision:
72	
73	> For optimal contrast and legibility, determine whether to add a **dimming layer** behind
74	> components with clear Liquid Glass: if the underlying content is bright, consider [adding
75	> one]… you don't need to apply a dimming layer [otherwise].
76	
77	**Scroll edge effects** are named as a separate legibility mechanism — "blurring and reducing
78	the opacity of background content."
79	
80	### It is not static
81	
82	> [Liquid Glass responds] to certain system settings, like if people choose a preferred look for
83	> Liquid Glass in their device's settings, or turn on accessibility settings that **reduce
84	> transparency** or **increase contrast**.
85	
86	A design that assumes the glass look is fixed will break under Reduce Transparency and Increase
87	Contrast. Both are design-time states to art-direct, not runtime accidents — the same rule
88	`§12` applies to reduced motion.
89	
90	---
91	
92	## Material 3 Expressive — verified
93	
94	**It is not a new version and M3 is not deprecated.** Google states this directly:
95	
96	> to be clear — M3 Expressive isn't a new version of the system. We're not deprecating M3.
97	
98	It is "an evolution… a set of new features, updated components, and design tactics."
99	
100	### The research basis, which is unusually strong for design guidance
101	
102	> M3 Expressive is our most researched update to the design system since its launch in 2014.
103	> Extensive user research — **46 studies with more than 18,000 participants**.
104	
105	Stated takeaways:
106	
107	- Expressive designs are **preferred by people of all ages**
108	- They score higher on user attention
109	- **"participants spotting key UI elements up to four times faster in expressive screens"**
110	
111	That last one is the load-bearing number, and it is the rare case where an *expressive* choice
112	is defended on usability grounds rather than taste. It belongs in `STYLES.md` as a counterweight
113	to the reflex that restraint is always safer.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## VoiceOver as a design decision — verified
118	
119	The VoiceOver page is **new as of March 7, 2025** (split out of the main accessibility page).
120	Its content is design-time, not code-time:
121	
122	> **Provide alternative labels for all key interface elements.** [Standard elements] have
123	> generic labels by default, but you should provide more descriptive labels that convey your
124	> app's functionality. Add labels to any custom elements your app defines.
125	
126	The genuinely design-shaped rule, and the one that has no web checklist equivalent:
127	
128	> **Specify how elements are grouped, ordered, or linked.** Proximity, alignment, and other
129	> visible contextual cues help sighted people perceive the relationships between elements.
130	
131	With Apple's own worked example: in an **ungrouped** layout "VoiceOver describes each image
132	before moving on to the captions"; in a **grouped** one it describes each image with its caption.
133	
134	**This is the point.** Visual proximity silently encodes relationship for sighted users. That
135	relationship does not exist for VoiceOver unless someone *declares* it — and whoever decides
136	that images and captions belong together is the designer, at layout time, not a developer
137	patching later. Default reading order in US English is top-to-bottom, left-to-right.
138	
139	**Rotor support** is the native analogue of heading/landmark navigation: identify headings and
140	key elements so people can jump by type rather than traverse linearly.
141	
142	---
143	
144	## What goes where
145	
146	| Finding | File |
147	|---|---|
148	| Liquid Glass: functional layer only, never content layer | `SURFACES.md`, as a hard rule |
149	| Regular vs clear variant decision + the dimming-layer follow-on | `SURFACES.md` decision procedure |
150	| Reduce Transparency / Increase Contrast as designed states | `ACCESS.md` + `CRAFT.md` three-states |
151	| M3 Expressive: not a new version; 46 studies / 18,000 participants; 4× faster element spotting | `STYLES.md` |
152	| VoiceOver grouping as a layout-time decision | `ACCESS.md`, Loop 1 |
153	| The fabrication finding | `PRINCIPLES.md` — sourcing rule for anything the plugin quotes |
154	
155	## Still open on this topic
156	
157	Navigation models per platform (tab bar vs bottom nav, predictive back), safe-area and
158	edge-to-edge specifics including the Android 15 change, gesture conflicts with author-built
159	swipe, and TalkBack. The cached claims cover these but none is verified.

1	# Verified — tablet and desktop as their own disciplines
2	
3	**Date:** 2026-08-01
4	**Method:** rendered DOM read off the live primary sources with a headless browser. Every
5	number and every absence below was checked on the page, not recalled.
6	
7	This topic was a **total blank** in all three parent repos — "tablet" appeared twice, both
8	times as a number in a screenshot checklist.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## The finding that invalidates most existing guidance
13	
14	**Split View, Slide Over, and Stage Manager no longer exist in Apple's design guidance.**
15	
16	Searched the current Multitasking page for each term:
17	
18	| Term | Occurrences |
19	|---|---|
20	| Split View | **0** |
21	| Slide Over | **0** |
22	| Stage Manager | **0** |
23	| windowed | 4 |
24	| tiling | 1 |
25	
26	Change log on that page: **June 9, 2025 — "Reorganized guidance in platform considerations,
27	and added guidance for multitasking with multiple windows in iPadOS."**
28	
29	What replaced them, in Apple's words:
30	
31	> People can use iPad with either full-screen or windowed apps. When full screen, apps occupy
32	> the full screen, and people can switch between individual app windows using the app
33	> switcher… with behavior **similar to macOS**. The system provides window controls for
34	> common tiling configurations, entering full screen, minimizing, and closing windows.
35	
36	**iPad multitasking is now a macOS-shaped windowing model.** Any guidance teaching the
37	three-mode Split View / Slide Over / Stage Manager vocabulary is teaching a superseded
38	system. I would have written those three from memory without hesitating — this is the
39	clearest justification in the whole project for researching rather than recalling.
40	
41	### The design rule that follows, stated by Apple
42	
43	> **Apps don't control multitasking configurations or receive any indication of the ones that
44	> people choose.**
45	
46	You cannot detect the mode and you cannot request one. So a tablet design is not "a layout
47	for a tablet" — it is a layout that must be correct at **any width the user drags it to**,
48	with no notification that it changed.
49	
50	And the resize rule, which is the opposite of the mobile-first reflex:
51	
52	> As someone resizes a window, **defer switching to a compact view for as long as possible.
53	> Design for a full-screen view first**, and only switch to a compact view when a version of
54	> the content no longer fits.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## Material: five breakpoints, not three
59	
60	Most references cite compact / medium / expanded. There are five.
61	
62	| Breakpoint | Width | Common devices |
63	|---|---|---|
64	| **Compact** | under 600dp | phone in portrait |
65	| **Medium** | 600–839dp | tablet in portrait, foldable in portrait (unfolded) |
66	| **Expanded** | 840–1199dp | phone in landscape, foldable in landscape (unfolded), desktop |
67	| **Large** | 1200–1599dp | desktop |
68	| **Extra-large** | 1600dp+ | desktop, ultra-wide monitors |
69	
70	Note two things a naive reading misses: a **phone in landscape is Expanded**, the same class
71	as a desktop; and **medium is a tablet in portrait**, not a tablet generally.
72	
73	### Panes per breakpoint — the actual layout decision
74	
75	| Breakpoint | Panes |
76	|---|---|
77	| Compact | 1 |
78	| Medium | 1 (recommended) or 2 |
79	| Expanded | 1 or **2 (recommended)** |
80	| Large | 1 or **2 (recommended)** |
81	| Extra-large | **3** |
82	
83	Material names the failure directly:
84	
85	> **Additional space doesn't just mean making the same thing bigger.**
86	
87	That is the stretched-phone-layout failure, stated by the primary source. The escape is
88	stated too — extra width **reveals** rather than **stretches**: a collapsed navigation rail
89	expands, and a second pane appears showing what was previously a separate screen (a
90	messaging list gains the conversation beside it).
91	
92	### Height breakpoints exist and usually don't matter
93	
94	Compact/medium/expanded also exist for height, but Material says it plainly: *"since most
95	layouts contain vertically scrolling content, it's rare that layouts need to adjust."* Worth
96	one line in the plugin, not a system.
97	
98	---
99	
100	## Apple size classes
101	
102	A coarser system than Material's: each dimension is **regular** or **compact**, where regular
103	means a larger screen or a screen in landscape. Every current iPad model is
104	**regular-width, regular-height in both orientations**, which is why size classes alone are
105	insufficient for iPad layout now that windows resize freely — the size class does not change
106	as the user drags the window narrower.
107	
108	**Consequence:** on iPadOS, design against *available width*, not against the size class.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## macOS windows — three states, and they are visual
113	
114	> A macOS window can have one of three states: **Main** … **Key** … **Inactive**.
115	
116	The key window is the one receiving keyboard input, and it *"uses color in the title bar
117	options for closing, minimizing, and zooming; inactive windows and main windows that aren't
118	key use gray."* A window becomes key only when someone clicks its title bar or a component
119	requiring keyboard input.
120	
121	Design obligations that have no web equivalent:
122	
123	- **Three window states to design, not one.** A web page has no concept of being visible but
124	  not focused, with a different chrome treatment.
125	- **Window controls sit at the leading edge of the toolbar** — *"Make sure window controls
126	  don't overlap toolbar items."* A custom title bar that ignores this collides with the
127	  system.
128	- **Avoid putting critical information or actions** where window chrome may cover it.
129	- Custom windows must use system-defined appearances, or the state transitions must be
130	  hand-implemented: *"appearances update automatically… if you use custom implementations,
131	  you need to do this work yourself."*
132	- Primary vs auxiliary windows are distinct types with distinct rules.
133	
134	## tvOS safe area, since it is a hard number
135	
136	> Inset primary content **60 points** from the top and bottom of the screen, and **80 points**
137	> from the sides.
138	
139	Out of our four-surface scope, but it is the only overscan number in the corpus and costs one
140	line to carry.
141	
142	---
143	
144	## What this changes in the plugin
145	
146	1. **Tablet is not a breakpoint, it is a resize contract.** The surface-class fork needs a
147	   third question for tablet/desktop: *what is the narrowest and widest this can be dragged
148	   to, and is every width between them correct?* There is no notification and no control.
149	2. **`SURFACES.md` carries both breakpoint systems** — Material's five with dp values, and
150	   Apple's regular/compact with the warning that it does not change on iPad resize.
151	3. **The reveal-vs-stretch rule** goes in `STYLES.md` beside style-under-density. Extra width
152	   reveals a pane or expands a rail; it does not widen a column.
153	4. **Desktop gets window states** — main, key, inactive — as a required state set for
154	   desktop-shaped surfaces, the same way tool-shaped surfaces get the nine data states.
155	5. **Delete any Split View / Slide Over / Stage Manager language** before it is ever written.
156	
157	## Not yet covered here
158	
159	Windows/Fluent conventions, Electron and Tauri specifics, keyboard shortcut divergence
160	between macOS and Windows, and Android's large-screen quality guidelines. Those remain open.

1	# Verified platform numbers — targets, type, contrast
2	
3	**Date:** 2026-08-01
4	**Method:** rendered DOM text pulled with a headless browser from the primary source itself,
5	then read in context. **Not** WebFetch summaries — the earlier research run caught
6	summarizers returning fabricated normative wording twice, so every number here was read off
7	the live page.
8	
9	`curl` is useless for these: Apple HIG and m3.material.io are JS-rendered and return a
10	~160-character shell to a plain fetch.
11	
12	---
13	
14	## The correction that matters most
15	
16	**"Apple's minimum touch target is 44×44 pt" is wrong**, and it is repeated nearly
17	everywhere including in most design skills.
18	
19	Apple's own Accessibility page (change log: *June 9, 2025*) publishes **two** numbers per
20	platform, and 44 is the *default*, not the minimum:
21	
22	| Platform | Default control size | **Minimum** control size |
23	|---|---|---|
24	| iOS, iPadOS | 44×44 pt | **28×28 pt** |
25	| macOS | 28×28 pt | **20×20 pt** |
26	| tvOS | 66×66 pt | **56×56 pt** |
27	| visionOS | 60×60 pt | **28×28 pt** |
28	| watchOS | 44×44 pt | **28×28 pt** |
29	
30	> Offer sufficiently sized controls. Controls that are too small are hard for many people to
31	> interact with and select. Strive to meet the recommended minimum control size for each
32	> platform.
33	
34	Why this matters for us: a rule that says "44pt minimum on iOS" will be *cited as Apple's
35	requirement* and it is not. Ship the pair — default and floor — or the plugin is confidently
36	wrong in a way that is trivially checkable.
37	
38	## The four target numbers are four different things
39	
40	| Standard | Number | Applies to |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **WCAG 2.5.8** (AA) | 24×24 CSS px effective area | web, satisfiable by size **or** the geometric spacing exception |
43	| **Apple iOS/iPadOS** | 44×44 pt default, 28×28 pt floor | native iOS controls |
44	| **Material** | **48×48 dp** | touch targets |
45	| **Material** | **44×44 dp** | *pointer* targets — a separate, smaller spec |
46	
47	Material states the touch and pointer numbers separately:
48	
49	> For most platforms, consider making touch targets at least 48 x 48dp.
50	
51	> Consider making pointer targets minimums 44 x 44dp.
52	
53	Material also anchors the touch number in physical space rather than pixels — *"The
54	recommended target size for touchscreen elements is 7-10mm"* — and notes iOS's 44 itself.
55	
56	**The decision procedure this produces:** a cross-platform-neutral design takes **48dp /
57	44pt**, which clears every floor above. A platform-committed design may go to its own
58	default. Nothing goes to a platform *minimum* without a stated reason, because the minimum
59	is a floor for constrained cases, not a target.
60	
61	### Spacing is a separate obligation from size
62	
63	Material: **8dp** between targets.
64	
65	> In most cases, targets separated by 8dp of space or more promote balanced information
66	> density and usability.
67	
68	Apple, more specifically, and this is a rule almost nobody encodes:
69	
70	> In general, it works well to add about **12 points** of padding around elements that
71	> include a bezel. For elements **without** a bezel, about **24 points** of padding works
72	> well around the element's visible edges.
73	
74	A bezel-less control needs *double* the padding of a bezelled one. That is a checkable rule
75	and it belongs in the density section.
76	
77	Material also names the trap that makes small targets look compliant:
78	
79	> an icon may appear to be 24 x 24dp, but the padding surrounding it comprises the full
80	> 48 x 48dp touch target
81	
82	So the **icon size and the target size are independent decisions.** A 24dp icon in a 48dp
83	target is correct; a 24dp icon that *is* the target is a failure.
84	
85	---
86	
87	## Apple type sizes — default and minimum, per platform
88	
89	| Platform | Default | Minimum |
90	|---|---|---|
91	| iOS, iPadOS | 17 pt | 11 pt |
92	| macOS | 13 pt | 10 pt |
93	| tvOS | 29 pt | 23 pt |
94	| visionOS | 17 pt | 12 pt |
95	| watchOS | 16 pt | 12 pt |
96	
97	> Use recommended defaults for custom type sizes. Each platform has different default and
98	> minimum sizes for system-defined type styles to promote readability.
99	
100	And the scaling obligation, which is the one that actually breaks layouts:
101	
102	> Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least **200 percent** (or **140
103	> percent** in watchOS apps).
104	
105	A layout that cannot survive 200% text is not an accessibility bug found in QA — it is a
106	layout decision made at design time. This is exactly the audit's "accessibility is a
107	verification concern" failure, and it belongs in Loop 1.
108	
109	## Apple's contrast table — and that it names APCA
110	
111	Apple cites **both** WCAG and APCA, then states what its own tooling enforces:
112	
113	> Two popular standards of measure for color contrast are the Web Content Accessibility
114	> Guidelines (WCAG) and the Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm (APCA). Accessibility
115	> Inspector uses the following values from WCAG Level AA.
116	
117	| Text size | Weight | Minimum ratio |
118	|---|---|---|
119	| Up to 17 pt | all | 4.5:1 |
120	| 18 pt | all | 3:1 |
121	| any | bold | 3:1 |
122	
123	Note the boundary is **17 pt**, not the web's 18px/14pt-bold convention. A design system
124	that carries one contrast rule across web and iOS is using the wrong breakpoint on one of
125	them.
126	
127	## Reduce Motion — Apple names the techniques, not just the setting
128	
129	Most guidance says "respect `prefers-reduced-motion`." Apple says what to actually do, and
130	these are design instructions:
131	
132	> - Tightening animation springs to reduce bounce effects
133	> - Tracking animations directly with people's gestures
134	> - Avoiding animating depth changes in z-axis layers
135	> - Replacing transitions in x-, y-, and z-axes with fades to avoid motion
136	> - Avoiding animating into and out of blurs
137	
138	This is the "designed reduced-motion state" that `§12` demands, spelled out. The last two are
139	the ones that get missed — a z-axis or blur transition is exactly what a motion-sensitive
140	person cannot tolerate, and both are fashionable right now.
141	
142	## Other design-time obligations found on the page
143	
144	- **Gesture alternatives are mandatory, not optional.** "If you use a swipe gesture to
145	  dismiss a view, also make a button available." A swipe-only interaction is a design defect.
146	  This is the native analogue of WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements.
147	- **Time-boxed UI.** "Views and controls that auto-dismiss on a timer can be problematic…
148	  Prefer dismissing views with an explicit action."
149	- **Assistive Access** (iOS/iPadOS) is a distinct layout mode a designer must plan for:
150	  identify core functionality, one interaction per screen, confirm twice on
151	  hard-to-recover actions.
152	- **Accessibility Nutrition Labels** now exist on the App Store — accessibility support is
153	  publicly declared, which changes it from an internal quality bar to a marketing surface.
154	
155	---
156	
157	## What goes where
158	
159	| Finding | File |
160	|---|---|
161	| Default-vs-minimum target tables, all platforms | `SURFACES.md` |
162	| The four-standards target table + cross-platform 48dp/44pt rule | `SURFACES.md`, as the decision procedure |
163	| Bezel 12pt / bezel-less 24pt padding | `STYLES.md` style-under-density |
164	| Icon size ≠ target size | new icons section |
165	| Type default/minimum tables + the 200% rule | `SURFACES.md` + `ACCESS.md` |
166	| Apple's 17pt contrast boundary vs web's | `ACCESS.md` — flag the cross-platform mismatch |
167	| The five Reduce Motion techniques | `CRAFT.md` motion, as the designed reduced-motion spec |
168	| Gesture alternatives, time-boxed UI | `ACCESS.md`, Loop 1 decisions |
169

171	
172	Everything in `_mobile-raw-claims.md` and `_weba11y-raw-claims.md` that is not restated
173	above. Those files are extraction output from research runs that died before their
174	adversarial verification pass. Liquid Glass, Material 3 Expressive, predictive back,

All four workflows are resumed and running — they replayed their cached agents and picked up at the verification stage, which is the 75-agent bulk that none of them ever reached.

While they work, I'm covering the topics they *aren't* assigned, so nothing duplicates. Design tokens is done and verified:

**The name matters.** It's a **Community Group Draft dated 30 July 2026** — two days old — not a W3C Recommendation. Calling it "the W3C design token standard" would be wrong in exactly the same checkable way as the 44pt claim. The plugin pins the draft by date, because value shapes have already changed between drafts.

**Two shapes break naive token files.** `dimension` is an **object**, not a string — `{value: 16, unit: "px"}` — and the unit set is closed to **px and rem only**. Same for `duration` (ms or s).

**That closed unit set collides head-on with the platform research I just did.** Apple specifies in `pt`, Material in `dp` and `sp`. **None of them is expressible in a DTCG dimension.** So `tokens.json` is a *web* artifact, full stop. Native numbers have to ride in `DIRECTION.md` or an `$extensions` block, and the plugin will say that limit out loud rather than pretending one file serves all four surfaces. That's the kind of thing that would have surfaced as a bug six months into using it.

One more structural catch: an object **cannot be both a token and a group**, so the intuitive `color.brand` plus `color.brand.hover` nesting is illegal. That pushes a naming decision up into design time.

I also corrected the date stamps across the docs — I'd been writing 2026-07-28 and today is 2026-08-01.

Remaining unassigned topics I'll keep working while the workflows run: icons, deliberate rule-breaking, and industry verticals.
